problem: Embodied-AI benchmarks built on simulators such as Habitat, AI2-THOR and VirtualHome focus on largely collision-free navigation. When they include interaction, it is non-physical: objects simply attach to the agent. iGibson's interactive navigation is short-horizon and does not require changing the state of many objects. No benchmark offered a long-horizon, visually guided task-and-motion-planning (TAMP) task with realistic physics and a clear metric.
motivation: Household robots have to change the physical state of many objects under real physical constraints. Examples: arms may fail to reach, and held objects fall when the robot collides with something. Existing simulated tasks do not test this. The paper argues that navigation and interaction must be combined, that the agent must reason about using a tool (a container), and that both navigation and interaction must be physics-aware. These call for a new benchmark in a fully physics-driven simulator (ThreeDWorld).
key_idea: The paper defines a long-horizon rearrangement ('transport') benchmark in ThreeDWorld. A two-armed Magnebot with physics-driven magnets must explore multi-room houses, find 6-8 target objects and optional containers, and carry them to a goal furniture surface within 1000 steps. It uses a high-level physics-driven navigation/interaction API and a transport-rate metric.
insight: End-to-end PPO (Pure RL, 0.12 transport rate) essentially fails on this long-horizon, sparse-reward, physically constrained task. Putting exploration inside a rule-based hierarchical planner with A* low-level planning improves results sharply. Predicting waypoints (Frontier/Active/Semantic, 0.50-0.52) beats predicting low-level actions (RL Exploration, 0.33): the action-level RL agent explores but often collides with obstacles and fails to grasp. Learned waypoint exploration (Active Neural SLAM, SemExp-style) shows no clear gain over non-learned frontier exploration (0.51/0.52 vs 0.50). The authors attribute this to layout shift between seen and unseen houses and to maps that carry no physics information.
method: TDW-House dataset: 15 artist-built physically simulated houses (6-8 rooms each, ~50 object categories, all movable objects physics-driven), split into 10 seen (training) / 5 unseen (test) houses; 1000 training tasks and 100 test tasks (20 per unseen house).

Task definition: a goal spec such as 'vase:2, bowl:2, jug:1; bed' with 6-8 target objects of 5 types, randomly placed across rooms. Each room has a 25% chance of spawning a container, and one unique goal furniture item (sofa/bench/table/coffee table/bed) is chosen. Without a container the agent can carry only 2 objects (one per magnet arm).

Magnebot embodiment and physics-driven high-level API: two 9-DOF arms with magnet end-effectors, wheeled base, IK-based grasping. Discrete actions: move forward 0.5 m, rotate ±15°, go_to_grasp, put_in_container, drop. Actions can fail physically (unreachable, collision, tipping, dropped objects).
ActionStatus feedback: 18 status types (success, failed_to_grasp, collision, cannot_reach, not_in, ...) plus SceneState data, usable for reward shaping or planning priors; follows the OpenAI Gym API.

Baseline hierarchical agent: a rule-based high-level planner switches between sub-goals exploration → pick up container → pick up object → place. Switching rules: prefer the container; after 20% of the budget, pick up objects; after 90%, place; if no container, place once holding 2 objects. A low-level A* planner runs on a 0.25 m-cell occupancy map built from depth and a 3-channel semantic map (targets/containers/goal), re-planned every step.

Exploration variants: Pure RL (PPO end-to-end with task reward); RL Exploration (PPO outputs actions to maximize map coverage); Frontier (random unexplored waypoint); Active (Active-Neural-SLAM-style coverage waypoint policy); Semantic (SemExp-style waypoint policy rewarded for finding targets, containers and the goal). All policies are 4-layer CNNs trained with PPO for 10M frames.

setting.backbone: 4-layer CNN policies trained from scratch with PPO (Pure RL, RL/Active/Semantic Exploration) inside a rule-based high-level planner + A* low-level planner; Frontier baseline is non-learned
setting.training_data: 1000 generated tasks in 10 seen TDW houses; 10 million frames of PPO training per policy
setting.observation: egocentric 256x256 RGB + depth + ground-truth semantic segmentation mask (oracle perception); ActionStatus feedback
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward 0.5 m, rotate left/right 15°, plus high-level physics-driven interactive actions go_to_grasp / put_in_container / drop (IK-based); exploration baselines predict waypoints executed by A*
setting.privileged: oracle semantic segmentation masks; agent pose implicitly available from the simulator (maps are agent-centred); high-level IK grasp/put macros abstract away low-level control

numbers.backbone: 4-layer CNN waypoint policy (PPO, SemExp-style) + rule-based high-level planner + A*
numbers.extra: oracle semantic segmentation; 1000-step budget; mean ± 0.01 over 5 unseen houses (100 tasks)
numbers.evidence: Table 1 'Comparison of transport rate over 5 unseen rooms': Semantic Exploration 0.52±0.01

numbers.backbone: none (rule-based frontier waypoint sampling + rule-based high-level planner + A*)
4-layer CNN action policy (PPO, coverage reward) + rule-based high-level planner

numbers_note: This is a benchmark paper: all rows are baselines the authors implemented. Table 1 prints transport rate as a fraction (e.g. 0.52), converted here to 0-100. Active Exploration (0.51±0.01) is omitted for the 4-entry cap. Per-house transport rates appear only in a figure (Fig. 5) and are not reported numerically.
results: On 100 test tasks in 5 unseen houses (1000-step budget), no agent transports all target objects. The best baseline, Semantic Exploration, reaches a transport rate of 0.52. Active (0.51) and non-learned Frontier exploration (0.50) are nearly identical. RL Exploration reaches 0.33 and end-to-end PPO (Pure RL) only 0.12, showing that hierarchical planning with waypoint-level exploration is essential and that learned exploration adds little.
limitations: Uses oracle semantic segmentation and abstracted high-level IK grasp/put macros, so perception and low-level control are largely sidestepped; no sim-to-real or real-robot evaluation.
Small scale: only 15 houses (5 for testing, 100 test tasks), and all baselines rely on a hand-designed rule-based high-level planner with fixed budget thresholds.
Only rigid objects; learned exploration policies fail to generalize to unseen layouts and ignore physics information (the authors note deformable/soft bodies as future work).
